title: Pools, Rules, and Tools: A Template-Integrated Resource Architecture

methods.name: Four-module reader architecture: fonds_reader, rules_applier, tools_invoker, integration
methods.description: One Python reader module per resource category (data pools, governance rules, executable tools) plus an orchestrator that runs all three.
methods.evidence: This paper introduces template_pools_rules_tools, a meta-project exemplar that resolves this dilemma with a four-module archi- tecture (fig. 1). Each module handles one resource category plus a fourth orchestration module:

methods.name: Typed YAML manifests (fonds.yaml, rules.yaml, tools.yaml) for discovery
methods.description: Each shared resource exposes a typed manifest that its reader uses for discovery and validation; consumers never modify resources.
methods.evidence: Each resource exposes a typed manifest (fonds.yaml, rules.yaml, tools.yaml) that the corresponding reader module uses for discovery and validation.

methods.name: Repo-root-relative path resolution and graceful-degradation readers
methods.description: Paths resolve via pathlib parents[N]; readers check existence, catch yaml.YAMLError, log warnings and return empty values rather than raising.
methods.evidence: Graceful degradation: every reader checks file existence before parsing and catches yaml.YAMLError around the parse itself, logging a warning and returning a safe empty value either way.

methods.name: {{TOKEN}} injection of runtime statistics into the manuscript
methods.description: A script hydrates manuscript tokens from integration-run JSON just before pandoc renders, so counts in the prose come from the pipeline.
methods.evidence: Hydrate {{TOKEN}} values and inject them into output/manuscript/ immediately before rendering

methods.name: Real-file tests (no mocks), property-based tests and a negative control
methods.description: Nine test files exercise the eight src/ modules with real YAML/BibTeX files; one test monkeypatches the source to prove tokens are live-wired.
methods.evidence: Tests use real file paths, real YAML files, and real BibTeX content rather than mocks, ensuring that coverage numbers reflect genuine code paths through the resource-discovery logic.

key_findings: In a representative run, the integration demo loaded 3 fonds, validated 2 rule sets, discovered 3 tools and processed 8 bibliography entries.
The paper claims typed manifests shift failure detection from runtime to pipeline startup, which it frames as an improvement for reproducibility.
It proposes a three-level resilience design (resource absence, schema malformation, script absence) so the pipeline reports failures informatively instead of crashing.
The authors argue a manifest-and-reader pattern avoids the packaging overhead of shared libraries, the lost validation of symlinks, and the setup burden of environment variables.
Stated limitations include structural-only validation by default, no concurrency handling against parallel writers, and a small-scale design assumption.
key_findings_evidence: In a representative pipeline run, the integration demo loaded 3 fonds, validated 2 rule sets, discovered 3 tools, and processed 8 bibliography entries

A typed manifest convention (fonds.yaml, rules.yaml, tools.yaml) that makes resource capabilities explicit and checkable at pipeline initialisation time, shifting failure detection from runtime to startup
A three-level resilience design — resource absence, schema malformation, and script absence — that allows the pipeline to degrade gracefully and report failures informatively rather than crashing

The manifest-and-reader pattern adopted here — versioned typed manifests, repo-root-relative discovery, and graceful degradation — sits between these alternatives: no packaging overhead, structured validation, and zero required environment configuration.
The architecture tolerates absence gracefully; it does not guarantee atomicity against concurrent writers.
